comments.text:
If Europe can be recognised as a continent despite being physically connected to Asia, why can’t South Asia’s classification be challenged too?

Continental boundaries are not purely geological; history and convention shape how we divide the world. South Asia has a distinct geographical setting and a remarkably interconnected past. The Indus Valley civilisation, Gandhara, Ashoka’s inscriptions in present-day Afghanistan, and the Mauryan and Kushan empires reflect centuries of political, cultural and commercial connections across borders that exist today.

What if we recognised a proposed Indian Continent comprising eight countries?

- India
- Pakistan
- Bangladesh
- Afghanistan
- Nepal
- Bhutan
- Sri Lanka
- Maldives

These nations have distinct identities and were never one unified civilisation. Yet their histories intersect through trade, migration, religion, kingdoms and shared geographical networks, creating a regional world that predates modern borders.

Akhand Bharat is a historical-political idea. The Indian Continent is a proposed cultural-geographical framework, not a call to merge nations or claim their territories.

The question is not whether these countries should become one, but whether our inherited continental labels adequately reflect their connected history.

comments.text:
IMO, India united due to history and sociocultural influences. India as a whole, essentially fell from one occupier to another. The Mughalis came, and when they decayed, was replaced by the British in the most heavily populated places of India. Hence, there was a preexisting cultural narrative of self liberation from foreign rule that had time to foment across centuries. Mainland Indochina, throughout the same time period, lacked any of that until the British and French arrived in force.

Furthermore, British presence in India also led to introduction of British thought - much of it contributing towards Indianization and promotion of self rule and legitimizing the idea of eventual self determination. The introduction of common law, rule of law, rule of higher law, and liberal thought strengthened and institutionalized Indian will for self governance under the framework of a secular state governed by rule of law and constitutional rule, rather than one of tribal competition or dominance of a local kingdom over neighboring peoples, as was the case in mainland Indochina during the same time period.

Which brings us back to Indochina. The Khmer came and went. When they decayed, Mainland Indochina became split into 3 spheres - Tai (Siam/Thai), Vietnamese, and Malay proto-federation. The Malays mostly existed as self governing city states and kampungs and thus kept to themselves. It's the Thais and Vietnamese, however, which contributed to much of warfare, conquest, and imperialism in pre-European early modern Indochina history. Opposition to Central Thai kingdoms and Vietnamese kingdoms by the Lao and Khmer therefore served as a basis for their respective national idea, and the arrival of the French meant the Khmer and Lao, stuck between Thais and Dai Viets, welcomed the French as guarantors of independence from the Thais and Viets. And the bet paid off. Sure, they suffered under French colonial rule, but through it they secured international recognition as separate nations, independent from Thai and Vietnamese states.

The Bamars, meanwhile, couldn't even fully subjugate the many peoples of Myanmar. Not in early modern era, not even to this day. The most they did in that era was to occasionally fuck with the Thais.

In any case, a free for all between Bamars, Thais, and Viets with Lao and Khmer stuck in the middle meant that these various people had reason to hate each other and stick to their own national idea, and furthermore, leverage European presence as a counterbalance against indigenous land empires (Thai and Viet) within Indochina.
